subject: Archaeology
title: Mohenjo-daro: City Without a Name
description: A micro-lesson that makes Mohenjo-daro: City Without a Name usable.

hook.text: In the 1920s, archaeologists in Pakistan found a 4,500-year-old city with indoor plumbing and grid streets.

buildup.text: Mohenjo-daro was part of the Indus Valley Civilization, which rivaled Egypt and Mesopotamia in scale.

discovery.text: The city had a Great Bath, standardized weights, and advanced drainage — but no palaces or temples.

twist.text: Nobody can read the Indus script. Without decoding it, we cannot know the city's real name or rulers.

climax.text: The city was abandoned around 1900 BCE. Climate change and river shifts likely made it unlivable.

punchline.text: A city with perfect plumbing left no readable words behind.

quiz.question: Why do we not know Mohenjo-daro's original name?
options: All records were destroyed in a fire
The Indus script has never been deciphered
The city predates the invention of writing

details.summary: Mohenjo-daro, excavated in the 1920s in Pakistan's Sindh province, is one of the largest cities of the Indus Valley civilization, dating to around 2500 BCE.
details.whyItMatters: Mohenjo-daro demonstrates that urban planning, public sanitation, and standardized systems existed 4,500 years ago — rivaling contemporary Mesopotamian cities. Yet its civilization remains voiceless because no one can read its script.
takeaways: One of the largest cities of the Indus Valley civilization
Featured grid-planned streets and advanced sewerage systems
Its script remains undeciphered, leaving the civilization voiceless

faq.question: What is the Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro?
faq.answer: A large waterproofed brick structure measuring 12 by 7 meters and 2.4 meters deep, likely used for ritual bathing. Its sophisticated waterproofing — natural tar between brick layers

faq.question: Why did Mohenjo-daro decline?
faq.answer: Theories include shifting of the Indus River, repeated flooding, climate change, and disruption of trade networks. There is little evidence of violent destruction. The city may have been gradually abandoned as environmental conditions made urban life there unsustainable around 1900 BCE.
